threads (default 20 when `max_workers` is None). Unlike the other modes, where the
`ThreadPoolExecutor`/`MultiprocessingPool` workers are only exercised once strategies are
created, this means any code path that constructs a `ResultsStrategyFactory` with
`mode="thread-queue-parallel"` but never consumes (e.g., CLI validation, dry runs, tests
that don't call `shutdown()`) leaks 20 daemon threads. It also means `max_workers or 20`

The exception is only logged; the offset is then marked complete, so `get_committable_offsets()` will treat it as processed and the commit loop will advance past it. This means a message whose processing failed is permanently skipped (at-most-once delivery), directly contradicting the class docstring "Only commits offsets after successful processing" and the expectation in `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` that failed messages block commits. A realistic trigger: a transient DB error in `handle_result` causes the check result to be silently dropped and its offset committed. Either failed items should be retried/requeued, or their offsets must remain outstanding (with an unbounded-blocking-commit tradeoff made explicit).

File: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py, Line: 339, Issue: join() conflates close: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join()` calls `self.close()`, which shuts down the commit thread and the entire worker pool. Arroyo's `StreamProcessor` calls `close()` and then `join()` during graceful shutdown, so this is mostly benign, but if `join()` is ever called independently (e.g., after `terminate()`, or by framework code expecting join to only wait), it triggers a full shutdown as a side effect and ignores the `timeout` argument. Additionally, calling `queue_pool.shutdown()` twice (close then join, or terminate then close) re-invokes `q.shutdown()` on already-shut-down queues; it is swallowed by the broad `except Exception`, but the second `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` still adds up to 5s of unnecessary blocking per worker during shutdown.

File: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py, Line: 96, Issue: Unbounded offset tracking: `OffsetTracker.all_offsets` only prunes entries in `mark_committed`, and `outstanding` entries are only removed via `complete_offset`. If a single offset never completes (e.g., a worker dies or an item is stuck in a queue during shutdown), `get_committable_offsets` will never advance for that partition and the sets grow with every subsequent message for the lifetime of the process, and the `range(start, max_offset + 1)` scan in `get_committable_offsets` becomes progressively more expensive on every 1-second commit tick. Low severity in normal operation, but a stuck group key (poison message repeatedly failing is handled, a hung `result_processor` is not) makes both memory and CPU grow without bound.

findings: File: pkg/services/cleanup/cleanup.go, Line: 77, Issue: Frequency change: The cleanup ticker interval is reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This makes the cleanup job (which now runs batched SELECT + DELETE queries against the annotation tables) execute 10x more often. If this is intentional to complement the deadlock workaround in the annotations store, consider documenting it; otherwise it may be an accidental leftover debug value that increases database load, especially since the new delete strategy runs multiple queries per cycle.

File: pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go, Line: 531, Issue: Misuse of Error-level logging: The new cleanup paths log routine, expected progress via `r.log.Error` (e.g., "Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by count", "Tags to clean", and their "cleaned ..." counterparts). These are not errors — `err` is always nil at those points (it was already returned on the lines above), so every cleanup cycle emits multiple Error-level log lines containing the full list of batch IDs. Since the cleanup job now runs every minute, this will flood error logs/alerting pipelines in production and make real errors harder to spot. These should be Debug (or at most Info) level, and the trailing `"err", err` fields are misleading since err is always nil there.

File: pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go, Line: 533, Issue: Log flooding with full ID lists: Each batch logs the complete slice of fetched IDs (`"ids", ids`). With the default/large `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` (the new test exercises a batch size of 32767), a single cleanup pass can dump tens of thousands of IDs per log line, repeated every minute. Even at Debug level this is excessive; combined with the Error level used here it is a production log-volume hazard.

File: pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/cleanup_test.go, Line: 237, Issue: Hard-coded IDs assume empty table: `createTestAnnotations` now explicitly sets `ID: int64(i + 1)` for every annotation. This assumes the `annotation` table is empty when the function runs. `TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp` reuses a single `fakeSQL` across all subtests and relies on the `t.Cleanup` registered inside each subtest to wipe rows; if any assertion before the cleanup registration fails (e.g., the initial `assertAnnotationCount`), or if `db.InitTestDB` seeds/migrates any annotation rows, subsequent subtests will attempt to insert IDs that already exist and fail with a primary-key conflict. Deriving IDs from an existing max or omitting explicit IDs (and reading them back) would be more robust.

File: pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/cleanup_test.go, Line: 127, Issue: Test data leak on failure: In `TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp`, annotations are created and counted before `t.Cleanup` is registered inside the subtest. If `assertAnnotationCount` or `assertAnnotationTagCount` fails right after `createTestAnnotations`, the cleanup function is never registered, so rows (including up to 40,003 in the new batch-size case) leak into the next subtest, which will then fail on the hard-coded ID inserts. Registering the cleanup before creating the annotations would make failures isolated.

Additionally, since `action` values can contain underscores, a denial key for (action, name, parent) could theoretically equal a permission-style key for a different action, though that is less likely. Using distinct prefixes (e.g., `.perm_denial_`) and/or skipping the denial cache when name/parent are empty would remove the ambiguity.

The interface `GrafanaConfig` (packages/grafana-data/src/types/config.ts) declares it as `number | undefined`, and the backend sends a numeric value (`AnonymousDeviceLimit int64`, defaulting to 0) in the frontend settings payload. When boot config is populated from that payload, code assigning a number to this property will fail type checking (or require a cast) because the inferred type is `undefined`. Declaring it as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;` matches the interface and the actual runtime data.

The frontend type added in this PR (`anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined` in `GrafanaConfig`) suggests the intent was for the field to be absent/undefined when unset. Since the Go DTO cannot produce `undefined` for a plain `int64`, the frontend will always receive `0`, and any frontend logic distinguishing "no limit configured" from "limit is 0" will not work as the type implies. Consider using a pointer (`*int64`) with `omitempty`, or aligning the TS type with the always-present `number`.

File: pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go, Line: 44, Issue: Performance regression: Device tagging was moved from a background goroutine (with its own 2-minute timeout and panic recovery) into the synchronous `Authenticate` path. Consider keeping the write off the hot path or at least documenting the intentional latency trade-off.

File: pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go, Line: 144, Issue: Possible Bug: In `TagDevice`, the newly added `return err` after a `tagDeviceUI` failure changes control flow: previously a UI-tagging failure was logged and execution continued (returning nil), allowing the rest of `TagDevice` (e.g., tagging the API device kind) to proceed. Now any UI-tagging error aborts the function early, so a transient UI-tag failure (e.g., DB hiccup) also prevents API device tagging, and the error propagates to callers. In `client.go` the caller only aborts authentication for `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, so the error itself is downgraded to a warning there — meaning the early return gains nothing for that caller while skipping the remaining tagging work.
